title: How UX delivers returns for the business, and how to prove it
description: UX isn't a cost, it's a growth strategy. The business metrics UX moves (conversion, retention and CAC), how to measure each one and how to present the results to managers.

related.title: Clint Acquire
related.body: In practice: a landing page and a conversational flow that drove 79% of sales demand.

blocks.text: UX isn't just aesthetics: it's a growth strategy

Many managers still see UX as a cost, an “extra” in building the product. But the truth is that good UX Design directly impacts retention, conversion and revenue. Want an example? Amazon increased its revenue by 300 million dollars just by changing a button from “Register” to “Continue.”

If you're a UX Designer or Product Manager and want to show the real impact of UX on the business, this article will give you concrete metrics, practical examples and strategies to present your results convincingly. Shall we?
How UX impacts the main business metrics
UX can't just be about “improving the experience.” It needs to be tied to business KPIs and help the company grow. Here are some of the metrics most affected by UX:

blocks.caption: A UX improvement doesn't stay on the screen: it reaches conversion, retention and acquisition cost, and from there, revenue.

blocks.text: 1. Conversion (conversion rate, CR)
Every user journey needs to be optimized for conversion. That goes for e-commerce, apps and landing pages.

An e-commerce store noticed that many users abandoned their cart at the payment step. A UX analysis revealed that the checkout form was too long. After reducing the fields to fill in, the conversion rate went up 17%.

blocks.caption: Fewer fields, less friction: the form shrinks and the example's conversion goes up 17%.

items: A/B testing different versions of forms and buttons.
Heatmap analysis (Hotjar, Crazy Egg, Microsoft Clarity).

blocks.text: 2. Retention and engagement
Good UX makes users want to come back. If a product is complicated or frustrating, it will be abandoned.

LinkedIn noticed that many new users created profiles but didn't come back. To fix this, they redesigned the onboarding, suggesting connections and filling in data automatically. The result? A 20% increase in new user retention.

blocks.caption: The retention curve: with better onboarding, fewer people leave in the first weeks.

items: Cohort Analysis to understand whether users are coming back.
Average time spent using the product.
Bounce Rate (to see whether people leave too quickly).

blocks.text: 3. Lower CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost)
Better UX means more organic referrals and less need to invest in paid marketing.
Dropbox implemented a gamified referral system that grew its user base by 3900%, drastically reducing CAC.

blocks.caption: The referral loop: each satisfied user brings in the next one, and the cost per customer drops.

items: Compare acquisition cost before and after UX improvements.
Check the percentage of new users who came through referrals.

blocks.text: How to show the value of UX to managers
Now that you know UX impacts the business, how do you convince the decision-makers? Here are a few strategies:
avoid technical jargon and focus on financial impact.
present concrete numbers to prove improvements.

blocks.lead: Connect UX to the company's KPIs:
blocks.text: if the goal is to increase sales, show how UX improves conversion and retention.

blocks.caption: What convinces managers: the same KPI, before and after, tied to the UX change that explains the difference.

blocks.text: Conclusion: UX isn't a cost, it's an investment
Done well, UX Design drives growth, cuts costs and improves customer satisfaction. It's not just about making a website look nice, it's about creating efficient experiences that impact revenue.
Now tell me: have you managed to prove the value of UX at your company?
